name: The Allerton Jurassic Park Figs

location.address: Allerton Garden, Lawai Valley (tours depart from the NTBG visitor centre, 4425 Lawai Rd, Koloa, HI 96756)

access: Paid guided tour only, the Allerton Garden Guided Tour (adults $65, children 2 to 12 $32.50, about 2.5 hours, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday; prices rise in January 2027). Every tour includes a bus ride into the garden. Book ahead and arrive 30 minutes early.
transport: About 25 minutes by car from Lihue to the NTBG visitor centre on Lawai Road, where tours depart.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the buttress roots, rising like walls tall enough to walk between. They stand inside Allerton Garden, where the tour guide points out the spot used for Jurassic Park's raptor-egg scene.
verify_notes: Owner/manager of the ground (National Tropical Botanical Garden) names the Moreton Bay figs and their towering roots as a highlight and cites Jurassic Park. Ensemble not a single named specimen; one place to stand on the tour. Garden Island 2015 (Ryan Kazmirzack): Jurassic Park shot in Allerton Garden in 1992; most recognisable scene has Dr Alan Grant finding raptor eggs among distinctive roots of a Moreton Bay fig; 'so-called Jurassic Park trees' are a popular draw. No planting date, girth or height for these figs found in any fetched page; age left empty. Garden itself created from 1938 by Robert Allerton and John Gregg Allerton (Wikipedia); that is the garden's date, not these trees'. Pin is the NTBG visitor centre / McBryde side; Allerton valley with the figs is roughly 1 km south, exact fig spot unverified (no OSM node checked). ALIVE: NTBG tour page current (pricing notice for Jan 2027) and lists the figs; no tree-specific recent observation. Hurricane Lowell hit Kauai 2026-09-08 with islandwide tree damage; found no report on the figs, so alive-now thin: flagged. Single credible source (owner of the ground) plus one press item. Photo pass 2026-11-04 (approved): Commons file titled Jurassic Park trees of Allerton Gardens, National Tropical Botanical Garden, Kauai; the buttress-rooted figs fill the frame, daylight.
facts: NTBG: 'See the towering roots of the famous Moreton Bay fig trees featured in blockbusters like Jurassic Park' (https://ntbg.org/?p=30232)
Jurassic Park filmed in Allerton Garden in 1992; raptor-egg scene among fig roots (https://thegardenisland.com/?p=79090)
Guided tour only, $65 adult, ~2.5 h, Tue/Thu/Sat (https://ntbg.org/?p=30232)
story:
In Jurassic Park, Dr Alan Grant finds a clutch of raptor eggs among the roots of a giant tree. The tree is real, and it is one of the Moreton Bay figs in Allerton Garden on Kauai's south shore.

The Garden Island, the island's paper, recorded in 2015 that the film was shot here in 1992 and that the egg scene, its most recognisable moment in the garden, was filmed among the distinctive roots of a Moreton Bay fig. The garden's managers, the National Tropical Botanical Garden, still lead with them, promising the towering roots of the famous figs from the blockbuster. Locally they are simply the Jurassic Park trees.

What makes them screen-worthy is the buttressing. These figs stand on roots that rise out of the ground as towering walls, tall enough to walk between, and the guide stops among them to show where the scene was shot.

The garden itself was made from 1938 by Robert Allerton and John Gregg Allerton. That is the garden's date, not necessarily the trees', and nobody has published a planting date, girth or height for the figs. If you know when they went in, tell us.

Two honest cautions. Allerton is seen only on a paid guided tour, which starts with a bus ride into the valley. And Hurricane Lowell hit Kauai on 8 September 2026 with damage to trees across the island; we have found no report on these figs either way, so check with the garden before you book.

name: The Poipu Road Earpod

location.address: In front of Borthwick Kauai Mortuary, 3168 Poipu Road, Koloa, HI 96756

location_site.name: Borthwick Kauai Mortuary frontage, Poipu Road

access: Free to see from Poipu Road; the tree stands on the frontage of a funeral home in Koloa town. Keep to the roadside, and stay away during services.
transport: About 20 minutes by car from Lihue to Old Koloa Town.

official_register.name: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (Hawaii DLNR, via data.honolulu.gov), no. 1137

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the very large spreading tree in front of the Borthwick Kauai Mortuary on Poipu Road, Old Koloa Town. If the register is right, its seed pods are coiled into the shape of an ear.
verify_notes: SPECIES CONFLICT, kept in the story: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register 1137 says Earpod (Enterolobium cyclocarpum); Mayor Bryan Baptiste's letter (The Garden Island, 24 Dec 2007) calls the tree on the Borthwick Mortuary property a monkeypod (Samanea saman). Species follows the register; the story names both and asks the reader to check the pods. Register: girth 725.4 cm, height 54 ft, vitality Excellent, no assessment date, locality 'In Koloa along Poipu Road in front of the Kauai Mortuary, Inc.'. Mortuary street number 3168 from a search result only. No tree-level observation after Hurricane Lowell (2026-09-08). No age basis; Kauai forest-reserve plantings of the species 1926-1935 are a class fact, not bridged.
facts: Register: girth 725.4 cm, height 54 ft, vitality Excellent (Hawaii Exceptional Trees register 1137, CC0)
Mortuary is a Poipu Road landmark since 1928 (earlier lead note, Dignity Memorial result)
County exceptional tree list (2007 mayor's letter) includes a tree on the Borthwick Mortuary property, called a monkeypod (https://thegardenisland.com/?p=154994)
story:
Two official records agree that the big tree outside the Koloa funeral home is exceptional, and they disagree about what it is. Hawaii's exceptional trees register files it as an earpod. In 2007 Kauai's mayor, writing in The Garden Island, listed the monkeypod tree on the Borthwick Mortuary property among four south-shore trees on the county's exceptional list.

Both cannot be right, and the confusion is an easy one to make. Earpod and monkeypod are close relatives and often mistaken for each other. This page follows the register, which measured the tree, and leaves the question open. The way to settle it is the seed pods. An earpod's pods coil round on themselves into the shape of an ear, which is where the name comes from. If you stand under it and find pods of another shape, tell us, and send a photograph.

The register's figures are 7.25 metres round and 16.5 metres tall, and it rated the tree's vitality excellent. It gives no assessment date, so those numbers are as of some unknown visit.

The tree stands on the Poipu Road frontage of the mortuary in Old Koloa Town, in full view of the road. Nobody has dated it. Hurricane Lowell crossed south Kauai on 8 September 2026 and we have seen no report on this tree since, so if you pass, a sighting helps too. Please keep to the roadside when a service is on.

name: The Hongwanji Monkeypods

location.address: Honpa Hongwanji Mission / Koloa Early School parcel (TMK 2-8-004:056), Old Koloa Town, Koloa, HI 96756

access: Free to see from the public street. The trees stand on a shared Buddhist mission and preschool parcel; look from the road, as the preschool grounds are not open to the public.
transport: About 20 minutes by car from Lihue to Old Koloa Town.

official_register.name: Hawaii Exceptional Trees register (Hawaii DLNR, via data.honolulu.gov), nos. 1151 and 1152

how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a pair of large monkeypods side by side, broad flat-topped crowns of about the same size. They stand on the Honpa Hongwanji Mission and Koloa Early School lot in Old Koloa Town.
verify_notes: TWO SOURCES, FLAGGED for access and exact spot. (1) Register rows 1151 (girth 490.7 cm, 42 ft = 12.8 m, vitality Fair) and 1152 (girth 457.2 cm, 40 ft = 12.2 m, Fair), both TMK 2-8-004:056, locality 'Old Koloa Town, Honpa Hongwanji Mission and Koloa Early School'. Folded as one pair (twins metres apart per register wording; registers 1151, 1152). (2) The Garden Island, 17 June 2008 (Nathan Eagle): county Arborist Advisory Committee recommended adding 'a pair of monkeypods in Old Koloa Town' to the exceptional tree list; joint owners Honpa Hongwanji Mission and Koloa Early School had no objection; committee called them 'ideal specimens of older monkeypod trees' meeting criteria on location, size and aesthetic quality. Register heights/girths are at assessment, undated. Access: temple grounds are allowed under the rule, but the preschool shares the lot and I could not establish the exact boundary; whether the trunks stand on the Mission side or the preschool side is NOT verified. Pin = Old Koloa Town centre, not the trees. ALIVE: only the 2008 article and register; no recent observation; Hurricane Lowell (2026-09-08) struck south Kauai. Vitality only Fair. Recommend ship only if flagged and access line kept as given. 1150 (TMK 053, girth 487.7 cm, Excellent) is a neighbouring parcel monkeypod, not part of this pair: kept as a lead.
facts: Register 1151: 490.7 cm girth, Fair; 1152: 457.2 cm girth, Fair (Hawaii Exceptional Trees register)
Kauai Arborist Advisory Committee recommended the pair for exceptional status in June 2008 (https://www.thegardenisland.com/?p=152464)
story:
A Buddhist mission and a preschool share these two monkeypods, and in 2008 both said yes to having them protected. The Garden Island reported in June that year that Kauai's Arborist Advisory Committee had recommended adding a pair of monkeypods in Old Koloa Town to the county's exceptional tree list, calling them ideal specimens of older monkeypod trees on location, size and aesthetic quality. The joint owners, the Honpa Hongwanji Mission and Koloa Early School, raised no objection.

The state register now carries them as two entries on the same parcel. One is 4.91 metres round and 12.8 metres tall, the other 4.57 metres round and 12.2 metres tall, close enough in size to read as a matched pair. From the street they read as two broad, flat-topped crowns side by side.

Two cautions belong with them. The register rates both in only fair condition, and it gives no date for that assessment. And Hurricane Lowell crossed south Kauai on 8 September 2026; we have seen no report on these trees since. A visitor's photograph would settle more than any document can.

The parcel is a working preschool as well as a mission, and no source says on which side of that shared lot the trunks stand, so look from the street rather than walking in. Nobody has dated them either. If you know when they were planted, tell us.
